title: How to use AI to plan a team offsite that works
summary: In our study of 69 team gatherings, small, short offsites with time for planning rated most effective. Here's how to plan one with AI.
body_markdown:
Team offsites (or onsites, as they are sometimes termed in our age of distributed work) are table stakes in the modern organization. Whether you’re distributed, hybrid, or in the office, high-performing teams need[dedicated time together](https://www.atlassian.com/blog/teamwork-lab/ai-made-your-people-faster-but-its-your-office-thats-slowing-them-down) to plan, connect, and be creative.


But organizing these gatherings is expensive and logistically cumbersome, both for managers and team members who are traveling instead of working. That’s why the[Teamwork Lab](https://www.atlassian.com/blog/teamwork-lab) decided to identify what exactly makes an in-person meeting successful. (At Atlassian, we call them **intentional team gatherings, or ITGs** , to get around that tricky off- or on-site phrasing.)


The Teamwork Lab then used that research-backed framework to build an AI agent that serves as a central resource for planners at Atlassian.


### research at a glance


**What we did:**


- The Teamwork Lab gathered data from 69 engineering ITGs held between August and mid-October 2024.
- The team coded the agendas and used Rovo, Atlassian’s internal AI platform, to connect agenda data with survey outcomes.


**What we learned:**


- Successful gatherings have consistent, predictable patterns.
- They prioritize high-impact activities without over-scheduling the attendees.
- In-person gatherings require lots of documentation and are a good use case for an AI agent.


# Jump to:


- **What makes a team offsite successful?**
- **Putting research into practice with an AI agent**
- **How to build your own planning agent**

# What makes a team offsite successful?


The Teamwork Lab first identified what differentiates high-impact ITGs from those that fall flat. It gathered data from 69 engineering ITGs held between August and mid-October 2024.


The analysis included event characteristics from all the available ITGs, such as size and duration; 51 available agendas; and 56 post-ITG survey responses. Researchers manually coded a subset of the agendas to identify patterns, established keywords for each category, and used[Rovo](https://www.atlassian.com/software/rovo) to code all available agendas and connect agenda-time data with survey outcomes.


This analysis revealed consistent patterns across high-impact in-person gatherings:


- **Fewer people, fewer days:** Gatherings of 5–10 people held over two to three days consistently prove more effective than larger, longer events.
- **Don’t skimp on team building and planning:** Most teams devote surprisingly little agenda time to team building (7%) and strategic alignment/planning (20%), even though these two categories correlate most strongly with positive outcomes.
- **Leave room to breathe (don’t over-schedule):** Gatherings often fail because they’re over-scheduled and under-planned. Failing to build in breaks, buffer time, travel recovery, or accessibility needs leaves teams checked out before the real work begins.
- **Make outcomes concrete (and close the loop):** Underperforming gatherings suffer from vague goals. High-impact gatherings define specific deliverables up front and include a dedicated plan to capture decisions and next steps before everyone departs.


# Putting research into practice with an AI agent


Knowing what makes a great gathering is one thing – consistently designing one under deadline pressure is another. To bridge the gap between research and practice, the Teamwork Lab created **IRA (ITG Rovo Agent)** , an AI teammate built in Rovo to operationalize our findings.


Rather than leaving agenda design to guesswork, IRA serves as both a strategic guardrail and an administrative co-pilot:


- **Acts as an agenda architect:** IRA reviews draft agendas in real time, balancing time across connection, deep work, and planning while automatically flagging over-scheduling or a lack of buffer time.
- **Eliminates logistical friction:** IRA handles tedious prep work, generating “Know Before You Go” briefing docs, structuring calendar invites, and drafting team communications across chat and email.
- **Closes the loop:** Post-gathering, it prompts organizers to capture decisions and next steps before momentum fades, and it even generates a wrap-up blog.


If you’re an Atlassian, IRA is ready to use today—find it in Rovo or pull it into Slack via #help-itg. For everyone else, grab the prompt template below to spin up your own planning agent using this exact research-backed blueprint.


# How to build your own offsite planning agent


If you have[clear, documented resources](https://www.atlassian.com/blog/ai-at-work/want-more-confidence-in-ai-give-it-more-context) , building a planning agent is the next step. Based on our research, these are our recommended steps to create a stronger gathering:


1. Confirm the gathering goal, attendees, dates, location, and agenda.
2. Classify each planned activity using the five recommended activity types.
3. Create the agenda using planning guidance. Only finalize after the planner has reviewed.
4. Draft attendee communications and a “Know Before You Go” page.
5. Create calendar holds and send communications only after the planner has reviewed.
6. Generate a wrap-up blog with key outcomes, concrete next steps, and named owners.


## Try out a sample prompt/status


Once you’ve classified each activity, here is a sample prompt you can try.


### try this prompt


Help me design a draft agenda for an in-person team gathering, grounded in the five research-backed activity types below.


**Context**


- Team: \[team name\]
- Attendees: \[number, roles, locations / time zones\]
- Dates and working hours: \[e.g., Tue–Thu, 9:00 a.m.–4:00 p.m.\]
- Location: \[office / city / hybrid\]
- Primary objective: \[e.g., align on H2 roadmap and strengthen a newly merged team\]


**The five activity types — classify every agenda item as exactly one:**


1. Core Work — executing project work together (co-working, whiteboarding, collaboration time).
2. Alignment + Planning — setting direction, priorities, and decisions (roadmap, OKRs, vision, refinement).
3. Context + Skills — sharing knowledge or building skills (demos, lightning talks, AMAs, deep dives, training).
4. Team Building — a facilitated activity with an explicit goal of improving how the team works together (trust, communication, norms); has an owner and usually a debrief.
5. Social — unstructured time with no agenda or objective, purely for enjoyment and organic connection (meals, outings, free evenings, games).


The test for #4 vs #5: does it have a facilitator and a purpose beyond fun? Yes = Team Building. Just hanging out = Social.


**Please:**


1. Build the agenda so all five activity types appear, and deliberately protect time for Team Building and Alignment + Planning. Teams routinely under-invest here (roughly 7% and 20% of agenda time), yet these two correlate most strongly with successful gatherings — don’t let them get squeezed out.
2. Guarantee at least four hours of working time (Core Work, Alignment + Planning, or Context + Skills — excluding Social) per full day, but don’t overschedule: build in breaks, buffer time, meals, and travel/recovery so days aren’t packed wall-to-wall.
3. Tie the agenda to concrete outcomes: state a specific deliverable or decision for each working session, and end with a session to capture decisions, owners, and next steps before everyone departs.
4. Present the agenda as a table with: time, session, objective, activity type, owner, and expected output.
5. After the table, summarize total hours and percentage of time per activity type, and show the calculation for each percentage.
6. Flag any assumptions or missing information rather than inventing details, and call out if any activity type is missing or overweight.


# The bottom line


In-person gatherings are a significant investment, but the payoff is measurable:[Atlassian’s research found](https://www.atlassian.com/blog/innovation/intentional-togetherness-research) that **team gatherings boost team connection by 27% on average** . That lift fades over about four months — a pattern we call “connection decay” — which points to an optimal cadence of roughly three gatherings a year.


Getting that return depends on the agenda. The most effective gatherings set a clear goal, protect time for team building and planning, and leave room to turn decisions into next steps before everyone heads home.


An AI agent won’t replace a human planner, but it lifts the administrative weight and keeps the agenda anchored to what the research says works. Let it do the heavy lifting so your team can focus on the work you came together to do.


---


***Methodology:** The Teamwork Lab conducted the analysis in early 2025, based on 69 engineering ITGs held in late 2024. Cross-analysis between agenda activities and post-event outcomes includes the subset of teams that completed both the agenda breakdown (n=51) and follow-up survey (n=56).*
